steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a KNN variant that caps the allowed distance between training and test samples, so K is found per test sample, with indoor localization based on ion-mobility spectrometry as the application. Include a short paper-organization paragraph at the end.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- KNN background
- Classification and distribution mismatch between training and test samples
- Example: fingerprint-based indoor localization
- Proposed Flexible KNN
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- KNN background
  - widely used, well studied; simple, easy to implement, parameter-free
  - extension of nearest neighbor rule; suboptimal, error rate at most twice the Bayes rate
- Classification and distribution mismatch
  - test sample labels derived from training sample labels
  - same distribution: SVMs, Fuzzy and Bayesian classifiers, neural-network-based classifiers do well
  - slightly different distributions: these degrade, KNN and variants commonly used
  - main idea: find K closest training samples (predefined distance), infer class from theirs
- Fingerprint-based indoor localization
  - earlier study: weighted KNN beat several parametric classifiers with WLAN measurements when access point density high
  - low density: accuracy degraded considerably
  - reason: lack of training locations with same access points as test sample
  - choosing different K might help; many KNN variants optimize K
- Flexible KNN
  - sometimes optimizing K useless: no training samples close to test sample -> wrong label from any variant
  - examples: indoor localization (room/area without training data), medicine (disease without training data)
  - allowed distance limited from above; only samples within limit used
  - different K per test sample -> Flexible KNN (Flex KNN)
  - K=0: says no training sample close enough; more useful than untrustworthy label
  - no such variant published before (to authors' knowledge)
- Organization
  - Sec. 3 standard KNN + overview of variants; Sec. 4 Flex KNN; Sec. 5 comparison for IMS-based indoor localization; Sec. 6 conclusions and outlook

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The K Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier is a machine learning algorithm that is widely used and has been studied a lot, because it is simple, easy to implement and parameter-free. It extends the nearest neighbor rule, which is a suboptimal classifier with an error rate that is at most twice the Bayes rate.

In classification, the labels of test samples are derived from the labels of training samples. When training and test samples follow the same distribution, support vector machines, Fuzzy and Bayesian classifiers, and neural-network-based classifiers perform well. But when the distributions of training and test samples are even slightly different, these methods can degrade a lot, and KNN and its variants are commonly used. The main idea of KNN is to find the K training samples that are closest to the test sample with respect to some predefined distance measure, and then infer the class membership of the test sample from the class memberships of those K training samples.

Fingerprint-based indoor localization is one application where the distributions of training and test samples can be different. For example, in an earlier study the weighted KNN did better than several parametric classifiers for indoor localization with Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) measurements when the density of WLAN access points was high. When the density was low, the accuracy of the weighted KNN got considerably worse. One reason was that there were no training sample locations where the same access points were observed as in the test sample (see the earlier study for details). In this case a different K might help with accuracy, and many KNN variants that focus on optimizing K have been proposed.

- Flexible KNN
  - when no training samples are near the test sample, any KNN variant gives a wrong label, so optimizing K does not help
  - examples: indoor localization (room or area with no training data), medicine (disease with no training data)
  - cap the allowed distance from above; only training samples within the limit are used; K differs per test sample -> Flex KNN
  - K=0 -> tell the user no training sample is close enough, better than an untrustworthy label
  - not published before as far as we know
- Organization: Sec. 3 standard KNN and variants, Sec. 4 Flex KNN, Sec. 5 Flex KNN vs standard KNN for IMS indoor localization, Sec. 6 conclusions/outlook

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The K Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier is a machine learning algorithm that is widely used and has been studied a lot, because it is simple, easy to implement and parameter-free. It extends the nearest neighbor rule, which is a suboptimal classifier with an error rate that is at most twice the Bayes rate.

In classification, the labels of test samples are derived from the labels of training samples. When training and test samples follow the same distribution, support vector machines, Fuzzy and Bayesian classifiers, and neural-network-based classifiers perform well. But when the distributions of training and test samples are even slightly different, these methods can degrade a lot, and KNN and its variants are commonly used. The main idea of KNN is to find the K training samples that are closest to the test sample with respect to some predefined distance measure, and then infer the class membership of the test sample from the class memberships of those K training samples.

Fingerprint-based indoor localization is one application where the distributions of training and test samples can be different. For example, in an earlier study the weighted KNN did better than several parametric classifiers for indoor localization with Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) measurements when the density of WLAN access points was high. When the density was low, the accuracy of the weighted KNN got considerably worse. One reason was that there were no training sample locations where the same access points were observed as in the test sample (see the earlier study for details). In this case a different K might help with accuracy, and many KNN variants that focus on optimizing K have been proposed.

But sometimes even optimizing K does not help much. If there are no training samples in the close neighborhood of the test sample, any KNN variant will give the wrong class membership label for the test sample. Such situations happen for example in indoor localization (the test sample is from a room or area of a building where no training data was collected) or in medicine (classifying a disease that has no training data available). To handle these situations well and to avoid time-consuming optimizations, this paper proposes a KNN variant where the allowed distance between training and test samples has an upper limit. Only the training samples within the limit are used to infer the label of the test sample. In this way a different K is found for each test sample, so we call the proposed classifier Flexible KNN (Flex KNN). If K=0, Flex KNN just tells that no training sample is close enough to the test sample to give a reliable estimate of its class membership. In the authors opinion this is more useful than an untrustworthy label from KNN and its existing variants. As far as the authors know, no KNN variant like this has been published before.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 3 discusses the standard KNN in detail and gives an overview of proposed KNN variants. Section 4 introduces and explains the Flexible KNN. Section 5 compares the performances of Flex KNN and standard KNN for indoor localization based on ion-mobility spectrometry (IMS) measurements. Section 6 has concluding remarks and an outlook on further research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The K Nearest Neighbors (K NN) classifier is a widely used and thoroughly studied machine learning algorithm because of its simplicity, ease of implementation and being parameter-free [1]. It is an extension of the nearest neighbor rule, a suboptimal classifier whose error rate is at most twice the Bayes rate [2].

In classification, the label of so-called test samples is derived from the labels of so-called training samples. If the training and test samples follow the same distribution, then support vector machines, Fuzzy and Bayesian classifiers, as well as neural-network-based classifiers perform well. However, if the distributions of training and test samples differ even slightly, the performance of these methods can degrade significantly, and K NN and its variants are commonly used [3]. The main idea of the K NN is to find the K training samples that are closest, with respect to a predefined distance measure, to the test sample and to infer the class membership from the class memberships of these K training samples.

One application where differences between the distributions of training and test samples can be observed is fingerprint-based indoor localization. For example, in [4] the weighted K NN outperformed several parametric classifiers for indoor localization based on Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) measurements when the WLAN access point density was high. However, when the density was low, the accuracy of the weighted K NN degraded considerably. One reason for the lowered performance was the lack of training sample locations in which the same access points were observed as in the test sample (see [4] for details). In such a case, choosing a different K might help to improve the accuracy, and numerous K NN-variants that focus on optimizing K have been proposed.

However, in some situations even optimizing K is of little use. If there are no training samples within the close neighborhood of the test sample, then any K NN-variant will yield a wrong class membership label for the test sample. Examples of such situations can be found in indoor localization (a test sample from a room or area of a building for which no training data has been collected) or medicine (classification of a disease for which no training data is available). In order to handle such situations well and to avoid time-consuming optimizations, this paper proposes a K NN-variant in which the allowed distance between training and test samples is limited from above. Only training samples within the limit are used for inferring the label of the test sample. This way a different K is found for each test sample, and therefore the proposed classifier is named Flexible K NN (Flex K NN). If K=0, the Flex K NN simply yields the information that no training sample is close enough to the test sample to provide a reliable estimate of its class membership. In the authors opinion, this is more useful than an untrustworthy label provided by K NN and its existing variants. To the authors knowledge, no such K NN-variant has been published before.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 3 discusses the standard K NN in detail and gives an overview of proposed K NN-variants. The Flexible K NN is introduced and explained in detail in Section 4. In Section 5 the performances of Flex K NN and standard K NN are compared for indoor localization based on ion-mobility spectrometry (IMS) measurements. Section 6 contains concluding remarks and an outlook on further research.

References:
[1] A. Onyezewe, A. F. Kana, F. B. Abdullahi, and A. O. Abdulsalami, “An Enhanced Adaptive k-Nearest Neighbor Classifier Using Simulated Annealing,” I. J. Intelligent Systems and Applications, vol. 1, pp. 34–44, February 2021.
[2] R. O. Duda, P. E. Hart, and D. G. Stork, Pattern Classification, 2nd ed., Wiley-Interscience, 2001.
[3] Z. Bian, C. M. Vong, P. K. Wong, and S. Wang, “Fuzzy KNN method with adaptive nearest neighbors,” IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics, vol. 52 (6), pp. 5380–5393, June 2022.
[4] P. Müller, M. Raitoharju, and R. Piché, “A field test of parametric WLAN-fingerprint-positioning methods,” 17th International Conference on Information Fusion (FUSION), July 2014.
